questions.question: Compare Java arrays vs ArrayList. When should you use each? Cover primitives vs generics, fixed vs dynamic size, performance, and API surface.
questions.title: Array vs ArrayList in Java — Primitives, Generics, Resize, and When to Use Each
questions.direct_answer: **Arrays** (`int[]`, `String[]`) are **fixed-size**, support **primitives directly** (`int[]` stores ints with no boxing), have **covariant typing** (`String[]` is an `Object[]`), and provide **O(1) random access and O(1) length**. **ArrayList** is a **resizable-array wrapper** that only holds **objects** (`ArrayList<Integer>` boxes ints into Integer), offers a **rich API** (`add`, `remove`, `contains`, `subList`, `iterator`, `stream`), and grows **amortized O(1)** on append. Use **arrays** when: (1) you need **primitives without boxing overhead** (numerical algorithms, large data), (2) size is **fixed and known**, (3) you need **multi-dimensional data** (`int[][]` for matrices, 2D grids), or (4) you're interfacing with **native code or legacy APIs**. Use **ArrayList** when: (1) size is **dynamic or unknown**, (2) you need the **Collection API** (stream, iterator, sort, filter), (3) you want to **hold objects** (Generic types work cleanly), or (4) you're doing **regular business logic** (the 95% case). Key differences: arrays have **`.length`** (field, no parens); ArrayList has **`.size()`** (method). Arrays allow **covariant assignment** that can fail at runtime (`Object[] arr = new String[1]; arr[0] = 1;` throws `ArrayStoreException`); generics are **invariant** and catch this at compile time. Arrays can hold **primitives or reference types**; ArrayList can hold only reference types — primitives must be boxed (use **Eclipse Collections / FastUtil** for primitive-specialized lists if boxing overhead matters). For **converting** between them: `Arrays.asList(arr)` (fixed-size view, careful!), `List.of(arr)` (immutable), `new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList(arr))` (mutable copy), and `list.toArray(new T[0])` back to array. **Performance**: arrays are marginally faster (no wrapper indirection) but JIT usually eliminates the gap for ArrayList; memory difference is significant for primitives (int vs Integer = 4 bytes vs 16+ bytes per entry).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows the fixed vs dynamic size, primitive vs object distinction, the `.length` vs `.size()` gotcha, and the covariance hazard of arrays vs invariance of generics
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying ArrayList stores primitives (it doesn't; it boxes). Confusing `.length` with `.length()` (the former is for arrays, the latter for String). Not knowing arrays are covariant (a runtime-safety hazard)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss array covariance hazard with ArrayStoreException, mention primitive-specialized libraries (Eclipse Collections, FastUtil, Trove), note JIT can close the performance gap, and explain memory overhead of boxing

sections.title: Arrays vs ArrayList — Side by Side
sections.content:
| Property | Array (`int[]`, `T[]`) | `ArrayList<T>` |
|---|---|---|
| **Size** | Fixed at creation | Dynamic (grows / shrinks) |
| **Primitives** | Yes (`int[]`, `double[]`) | No (boxed: `ArrayList<Integer>`) |
| **Generics** | No (raw covariant types only) | Yes (parameterized `<T>`) |
| **Size accessor** | `.length` (field) | `.size()` (method) |
| **Read element** | `arr[i]` | `list.get(i)` |
| **Write element** | `arr[i] = v` | `list.set(i, v)` |
| **Append** | N/A (must resize manually) | `list.add(v)` (amortized O(1)) |
| **Insert middle** | N/A (manual shift) | `list.add(i, v)` (O(n)) |
| **Delete** | N/A (manual shift) | `list.remove(i)` (O(n)) |
| **Contains** | Linear scan (manual) | `list.contains(v)` (O(n)) |
| **Covariance** | Covariant (hazard) | Invariant (safe) |
| **Stream / iterator** | `Arrays.stream(arr)` | `list.stream()` |
| **Multi-dim** | `int[][]`, `int[][][]` | Nested lists |
| **Memory** | Lower (primitives, no wrapper) | Higher (object headers, boxing) |
| **Type safety** | Runtime (ArrayStoreException) | Compile-time (generics) |

sections.title: Array vs ArrayList at the API Level
sections.content:
```java
int[] primes = {2, 3, 5};           // fixed length, primitives OK
primes[2] = 7;

List<Integer> nums = new ArrayList<>();
nums.add(2); nums.add(3);           // grows dynamically, boxed ints
nums.remove(Integer.valueOf(2));    // remove by value, not index
```

sections.title: Arrays — When They Shine
ArrayList — The Default for Business Logic
Array Covariance — The Safety Hazard
sections.content:
Arrays are **covariant**: `String[]` is an `Object[]`. This is convenient but **unsafe**:

```java
String[] strings = new String[3];
Object[] objects = strings;   // covariant — legal
objects[0] = Integer.valueOf(42);  // compiles fine!
// java.lang.ArrayStoreException: java.lang.Integer at runtime
```

The JVM checks the actual element type at runtime, throwing `ArrayStoreException` when you violate the array's true component type.

**Why covariance exists in Java**: before generics (Java 5), methods like `Arrays.sort(Object[])` needed to accept arrays of any reference type. Covariance was the only way. It's a legacy feature from pre-generics Java.

**Generics are invariant** — `List<String>` is **not** a `List<Object>`:
```java
List<String> strings = new ArrayList<>();
List<Object> objects = strings;   // COMPILE ERROR
```
This is the correct type-safe behavior. Use wildcards (`List<? extends Object>`) when you need flexibility.

**Don't mix generics with arrays**:
```java
List<String>[] lists = new List<String>[10];   // COMPILE ERROR: generic array creation

// Workaround — raw or wildcard:
List<String>[] lists = (List<String>[]) new List[10];  // unchecked warning
// Or better, use nested lists:
List<List<String>> lists = new ArrayList<>();
```

**Bottom line**: generics + ArrayList is type-safe; arrays + inheritance is a runtime-safety hazard. Prefer ArrayList for generic-typed collections.

sections.title: Converting Between the Two
Primitive-Specialized Collections
sections.content:
ArrayList<Integer> boxes every int into an Integer (16+ bytes per entry plus overhead). For large primitive-heavy data, use **specialized libraries**:

**Eclipse Collections** — `IntArrayList`, `LongArrayList`, `IntIntMap`, etc.
```java
IntArrayList list = new IntArrayList();
list.add(42);          // no boxing
int x = list.get(0);   // returns primitive int
```

**FastUtil** (`it.unimi.dsi.fastutil`) — extensive primitive collections.

**Trove** — older but widely used: `TIntArrayList`, `TIntObjectHashMap`.

**When to use**:
- Numerical computation over large arrays.
- Bitmaps, histograms, frequency counts.
- Graph algorithms with integer node IDs.
- Any case where millions of boxed integers show up in profiling.

**Java's built-in alternatives**:
- `int[]`, `long[]`, `double[]` — fixed size but primitive.
- `BitSet` — compact boolean array.
- `IntStream`, `LongStream`, `DoubleStream` — primitive stream pipelines.
- `ByteBuffer` — off-heap primitive buffers for low-latency.

**Project Valhalla (preview in later Java)** — will bring primitive classes and generic specialization, eventually allowing `List<int>` without boxing. Not available yet in production.

**Rule of thumb**: if your profile shows `java.lang.Integer` allocations or a suspicious ratio of `Integer` to `int[]` in heap dumps, switch to primitive arrays or specialized libraries.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Arrays** are fixed-size, support primitives directly, use `.length` field, covariant (runtime check).
- **ArrayList** is dynamic, stores objects only (boxes primitives), uses `.size()` method, invariant (compile-time check).
- **Use arrays** for: primitives without boxing, fixed-size data, multi-dim matrices, performance-critical loops.
- **Use ArrayList** for: dynamic size, object collections, Stream/iterator APIs, business logic (95% of cases).
- **Covariance hazard**: `String[]` is `Object[]` — `ArrayStoreException` at runtime if misused.
- **Generics are invariant** — `List<String>` is NOT `List<Object>`; compile-time safe.
- **Generic arrays disallowed**: `new List<String>[10]` — compile error. Use `List<List<String>>` instead.
- **Memory**: `int[]` ~4 bytes/entry; `ArrayList<Integer>` ~24 bytes/entry (object headers + boxing).
- **`Arrays.asList(arr)`** returns a fixed-size view; can't add/remove.
- **`list.toArray(new T[0])`** is the preferred List→Array (JDK-optimized since Java 8).
- **Primitive-specialized**: Eclipse Collections, FastUtil, Trove for large primitive data.
- **`Arrays.stream(intArr).boxed().toList()`** — the idiom for `int[]` → `List<Integer>`.
- **Performance**: arrays slightly faster but JIT usually closes the gap; memory overhead matters more than CPU.
- **Project Valhalla** (future) will allow `List<int>` without boxing.
- **Rule of thumb**: prefer `ArrayList` for business logic; reach for arrays when you have a clear reason (primitives, fixed size, multi-dim, or perf profiling shows boxing overhead).

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Arrays** are fixed-size containers that support primitives natively. **ArrayList** is a resizable wrapper around an array that only holds objects. Pick based on your needs.

**Use arrays when**
- You need **primitives without boxing** (`int[]`, `double[]`)
- Size is **fixed and known**
- **Multi-dimensional data** (`int[][]` for matrices)
- **Performance-critical loops** (JIT optimizes arrays extremely well)
- Interop with native code or legacy APIs

**Use ArrayList when**
- Size is **dynamic or unknown**
- You need the **Collection API** (stream, iterator, sort, filter)
- You want to hold objects (generics work cleanly)
- Regular **business logic** — the 95% case

**Key differences**

**Size accessor**
- Array: `.length` (field, no parens)
- ArrayList: `.size()` (method)
- Common trap for beginners

**Primitives**
- Array: `int[]`, `double[]` — no boxing
- ArrayList: `ArrayList<Integer>` — boxes every int
- Memory: `int[]` ≈ 4 bytes/entry; `ArrayList<Integer>` ≈ 24 bytes/entry

**Covariance**
- Arrays are **covariant**: `String[]` is `Object[]`
- Convenient but **unsafe**: `ArrayStoreException` at runtime
- Generics are **invariant**: `List<String>` is NOT `List<Object>`
- Compile-time safety wins

**Generic arrays disallowed**
- `new List<String>[10]` — compile error
- Use nested `List<List<String>>` instead

**Converting**

**Array → List**
- `Arrays.asList(arr)` — fixed-size view (can't add/remove)
- `List.of(arr)` (Java 9+) — immutable copy
- `new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList(arr))` — mutable copy

**Primitive array → List<Boxed>**
- `Arrays.asList(intArr)` gives `List<int[]>` with ONE element (wrong!)
- Use `Arrays.stream(intArr).boxed().toList()`

**List → Array**
- `list.toArray(new T[0])` — preferred (Java 8+ optimized)
- Faster than `new T[list.size()]`

**List<Integer> → int[]**
- `list.stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).toArray()`

**Primitive-specialized collections — when boxing matters**
- Eclipse Collections — `IntArrayList`, `IntIntMap`
- FastUtil — extensive primitive collections
- Trove — older but widely used
- Use when profiling shows `java.lang.Integer` allocations dominating

**Java built-in primitive alternatives**
- `int[]`, `long[]`, `double[]`
- `BitSet` — compact booleans
- `IntStream`, `LongStream`, `DoubleStream` — primitive stream pipelines
- `ByteBuffer` — off-heap primitive buffers

**Performance**
- Arrays marginally faster (no wrapper indirection)
- JIT often closes the CPU gap
- Memory difference matters more: boxing overhead for primitive collections
- `ArrayList` has better API (stream, sort, filter)

**Common traps**

**1. `.length` vs `.length()` vs `.size()`**
- Array: `.length` (field)
- String: `.length()` (method)
- Collection: `.size()` (method)

**2. Arrays.asList on primitive array**
- `Arrays.asList(intArr)` returns `List<int[]>`, not `List<Integer>`
- Use `Arrays.stream(arr).boxed().toList()` instead

**3. Array covariance bug**
- `Object[] arr = new String[3]; arr[0] = 42;` compiles but throws ArrayStoreException
- Generics catch at compile time

**4. Fixed-size view from Arrays.asList**
- Can't add/remove; for mutable, wrap in `new ArrayList<>(...)`

**5. Generic array creation forbidden**
- `new List<String>[10]` — compile error
- Use nested lists

**Project Valhalla (future)**
- Will allow `List<int>` without boxing
- Primitive classes, generic specialization
- Not available yet in production

**Recommendation:** For **business logic** (the 95% case), default to **ArrayList** — dynamic size, rich Collection API, generics for type safety, plays well with streams and frameworks. Reach for **arrays** when you have a clear reason: **primitives** (numerical algorithms, large data where boxing costs hurt), **fixed size** known at creation, **multi-dimensional** data (`int[][]` for matrices), or **performance-critical** hot loops where JIT-optimized array ops win. Remember the **covariance hazard**: `String[]` masquerades as `Object[]` and will throw `ArrayStoreException` at runtime — generics catch this at compile time. For **converting**, use `list.toArray(new T[0])` (JDK-optimized since Java 8), `Arrays.stream(intArr).boxed().toList()` for primitive-to-boxed, and `new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList(arr))` for mutable conversions (plain `Arrays.asList` returns a fixed-size view). For **huge primitive data** where boxing overhead dominates, use **Eclipse Collections**, **FastUtil**, or **Trove**. Never use `Arrays.asList(intArr)` on a primitive array — it returns a singleton list containing the array itself, not the ints. The mental model: **arrays = primitives-friendly, fixed, covariant (risky)**; **ArrayList = objects only, dynamic, invariant (safe), API-rich**. In most Java code, ArrayList is the right default.

questions.question: Compare HashMap vs ConcurrentHashMap. Cover thread-safety, lock striping vs synchronization, iteration guarantees, and null support.
questions.title: HashMap vs ConcurrentHashMap — Thread-Safety, Locking Strategies, Iteration
questions.direct_answer: **`HashMap`** is **not thread-safe**: concurrent `put`/`get` can cause **lost updates**, **infinite loops** (pre-Java 8 during resize), or `ConcurrentModificationException` during iteration. **`ConcurrentHashMap`** is **fully thread-safe** for any combination of reads and writes. The implementation has evolved: **pre-Java 8**, `ConcurrentHashMap` used **segment locking** (a.k.a. lock striping) — the table was split into 16 segments, each with its own lock; threads hitting different segments didn't contend. **Java 8 rewrote** it: now each **bucket head** is effectively its own lock via `synchronized` on the bucket's first node, and reads are **lock-free via `volatile`** loads; writes use **CAS** (`compareAndSwap`) for the initial insert and `synchronized` only for collision chains. This gives near-`HashMap` read performance with real thread-safety. **Null support** — `HashMap` allows **one null key** and **any number of null values**; `ConcurrentHashMap` **forbids null keys and null values** (throws NPE) — the rationale is disambiguation: `map.get(k) == null` could mean 'not present' or 'present-but-null,' ambiguous in concurrent code. **Iteration**: `HashMap.iterator()` is **fail-fast** (throws `ConcurrentModificationException` if modified during iteration); `ConcurrentHashMap.iterator()` is **weakly consistent** (no exception; sees a snapshot-like view; may or may not reflect concurrent modifications). **`Collections.synchronizedMap(hashMap)`** is another option — single-lock wrapper around a `HashMap` — but it's **slower** than `ConcurrentHashMap` because all ops serialize on one lock; use only for legacy code. When to use which: **single-threaded**: `HashMap`. **Multi-threaded with reads >> writes**: `ConcurrentHashMap`. **Multi-threaded with frequent writes**: `ConcurrentHashMap` (still wins). **Legacy or simple scenarios**: `Collections.synchronizedMap` is fine but avoid. Extra `ConcurrentHashMap` powers: atomic **`compute`**, **`computeIfAbsent`**, **`merge`**; parallel bulk ops **`forEach`**, **`reduce`**, **`search`** (Java 8+).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows HashMap's thread-unsafety (including the pre-Java-8 infinite-loop resize bug), ConcurrentHashMap's bucket-level locking and CAS, null-handling differences, and fail-fast vs weakly consistent iterators
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying ConcurrentHashMap uses 'one lock for the whole map' (it doesn't). Saying HashMap is safe for concurrent reads (it's not — resize during read is unsafe). Putting null in ConcurrentHashMap
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Describe the Java 8 redesign (bucket-level synchronized + CAS + volatile reads), mention Collections.synchronizedMap as slower legacy option, discuss atomic compute/computeIfAbsent, and reference the fail-fast vs weakly consistent iterator distinction

sections.title: HashMap vs ConcurrentHashMap vs Collections.synchronizedMap
sections.content:
| Property | `HashMap` | `Collections.synchronizedMap(m)` | `ConcurrentHashMap` |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Thread-safe?** | No | Yes (one lock) | Yes (bucket-level) |
| **Locking** | None | Single monitor | Per-bucket `synchronized` + CAS |
| **Reads** | Not thread-safe | Serialized | Lock-free (volatile) |
| **Null key** | One allowed | One allowed | NPE |
| **Null value** | Any number | Any number | NPE |
| **Iterator** | Fail-fast (CME) | Fail-fast (CME); manual sync | Weakly consistent (no CME) |
| **Size** | O(1) | O(1), synchronized | O(n) approx (sum of counters) |
| **Read perf under contention** | N/A (unsafe) | Slow (serialized) | Fast (no lock on read) |
| **Write perf under contention** | N/A (unsafe) | Very slow (serialized) | Fast (per-bucket) |
| **`compute`, `merge` atomic?** | Yes (Java 8, single-thread) | Yes, but not atomic with iteration | Yes, fully atomic |
| **Parallel bulk ops** | No | No | Yes (`parallelism` parameter) |
| **Use case** | Single-thread | Legacy / simple multi-thread | Modern concurrent |

sections.title: Why HashMap Isn't Thread-Safe
ConcurrentHashMap — Java 8+ Internals
Null Handling — Why CHM Rejects Nulls
sections.content:
**HashMap allows null keys and null values**:
```java
HashMap<String, Integer> map = new HashMap<>();
map.put(null, 42);    // OK — one null key
map.put("foo", null); // OK — any null value
map.get(null);        // returns 42
map.containsKey(null); // true
```

**ConcurrentHashMap rejects nulls**:
```java
ConcurrentHashMap<String, Integer> cmap = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
cmap.put(null, 42);    // NullPointerException
cmap.put("foo", null); // NullPointerException
cmap.get(null);        // NullPointerException
```

**Why?** Ambiguity in concurrent context:
- `map.get(key) == null` could mean: (a) the key is absent, or (b) the key is present but maps to null.
- Single-threaded, `containsKey` disambiguates.
- **Multi-threaded, that's a race**: between your `containsKey` and `get`, another thread could remove the key. You'd make a decision based on stale info.
- By forbidding null, `ConcurrentHashMap.get() == null` unambiguously means 'key not present.'

**Migration tip**: if porting from `HashMap` to `ConcurrentHashMap`, replace null-value entries with a sentinel (empty string, special constant) or drop them. Same for null keys.

sections.title: Iteration Semantics — Fail-Fast vs Weakly Consistent
Atomic Operations — compute, computeIfAbsent, merge
Collections.synchronizedMap vs ConcurrentHashMap
sections.content:
**`Collections.synchronizedMap(hashMap)`** wraps a HashMap with one lock around every operation:
```java
Map<K, V> sync = Collections.synchronizedMap(new HashMap<>());
sync.put(k, v);    // acquires the single monitor
sync.get(k);       // acquires the single monitor
```

**Problems**:
- **Single lock**: every op contends; scales poorly.
- **Iteration requires external sync**:
```java
synchronized (sync) {  // manual external sync
    for (Entry<K,V> e : sync.entrySet()) { ... }
}
```
If you forget, you get CME under concurrent modification.
- **Compound ops are not atomic**:
```java
// NOT atomic — race between get and put
if (!sync.containsKey(k)) sync.put(k, v);
// Need to wrap: synchronized (sync) { ... }
```

**`ConcurrentHashMap`**:
- No external sync needed for iteration.
- `putIfAbsent`, `compute`, `merge` atomic.
- Scales to many threads.
- Minimal read overhead.

**When `synchronizedMap` is fine**:
- Low-contention scenarios.
- Legacy code migration.
- Small maps in rarely-accessed paths.

**When to always prefer `ConcurrentHashMap`**:
- Any non-trivial concurrency.
- Anywhere you'd otherwise hand-roll synchronization.
- Spring bean maps, caches, registries.

**Hashtable** (very legacy):
- Same as `synchronizedMap`, but ancient API.
- Every op synchronized on the instance.
- **Never use in new code** — use `ConcurrentHashMap`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`HashMap`**: not thread-safe; race conditions, lost updates, resize hazards.
- **`ConcurrentHashMap`**: fully thread-safe; bucket-level `synchronized` + CAS + volatile reads (Java 8+).
- **Pre-Java 8 CHM**: used **segment locking** (16 segments, each a mini-HashMap with own lock).
- **Java 8 rewrite**: per-bucket synchronized on the first node; lock-free reads via volatile; CAS fast path.
- **Null handling**: HashMap allows one null key and null values; CHM throws NPE on null.
- **Iterator**: HashMap is **fail-fast** (CME on modification); CHM is **weakly consistent** (no CME, may or may not reflect concurrent changes).
- **`Collections.synchronizedMap(hm)`**: single-lock wrapper; slower than CHM under contention; requires external sync for iteration.
- **`Hashtable`**: legacy, don't use; same semantics as synchronizedMap.
- **Atomic compound ops in CHM**: `putIfAbsent`, `compute`, `computeIfAbsent`, `merge`.
- **Parallel bulk ops (Java 8+)**: `forEach(parallelismThreshold, ...)`, `reduce`, `search`.
- **`size()` in CHM**: approximate; use `mappingCount()` for long-valued size.
- **Treeification** for hash-collision-heavy buckets (8+ entries → red-black tree).
- **Don't block** in functions passed to `compute`/`computeIfAbsent` — bucket is locked.
- **Don't call CHM methods inside CHM's compute/merge lambdas** — deadlock risk.
- **Migration from HashMap to CHM**: replace null values with sentinels; iterate-modify patterns still work (no CME).

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**HashMap** is not thread-safe; **ConcurrentHashMap** is.

**HashMap hazards under concurrency**
- Lost updates: two threads putting same key, one wins
- Resize race: pre-Java 8 could create infinite loops (CPU pinned at 100%)
- CME on iteration: fail-fast iterator throws if modified outside
- Unsafe even for reads during resize

**ConcurrentHashMap — Java 8 redesign**

**Reads are lock-free**
- `get` uses volatile reads of table and bucket
- Zero contention for reads

**Writes use CAS then synchronized**
- Empty bucket: CAS-insert the node (lock-free fast path)
- Occupied bucket: synchronized on the bucket's first node
- Only threads hitting the same bucket contend

**Treeification**
- Bucket with 8+ entries becomes red-black tree
- Worst case per-bucket: O(log n)

**Incremental resize**
- Multiple threads can help rehash
- Doesn't block all other operations

**Pre-Java 8 CHM**
- Used segment locking (16 segments, each a mini-HashMap)
- Threads hitting different segments didn't contend
- Java 8 went finer-grained: per-bucket

**Null handling — a key difference**

**HashMap allows nulls**
- One null key
- Any number of null values

**CHM forbids nulls — throws NPE**
- Rationale: disambiguation under concurrency
- `map.get(key) == null` could mean 'not present' OR 'present but null'
- In concurrent code, you can't safely use containsKey to disambiguate (races)
- CHM removes the ambiguity: null always means 'not present'

**Iterator semantics**

**HashMap — fail-fast**
- Throws `ConcurrentModificationException` on concurrent modification
- Even within single thread: `for (k : map.keySet()) map.remove(k)` throws
- Fix: use `Iterator.remove()` or `keySet().removeIf()`

**CHM — weakly consistent**
- No CME, ever
- Sees elements that existed when iterator was created
- May or may not see concurrent modifications
- For a true snapshot: copy the map

**Atomic compound operations — CHM's superpower**

**`computeIfAbsent`** — thread-safe memoization
- `cache.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> expensiveCompute(k))`
- If key present: return existing value (no lambda call)
- If absent: call lambda, store result, return it
- Two threads racing with same key → lambda called ONCE

**`compute`** — atomic read-modify-write
- `cmap.compute("counter", (k, v) -> v == null ? 1 : v + 1)`

**`merge`** — combine new with existing
- `cmap.merge(word, 1, Integer::sum)` — thread-safe word count

**`putIfAbsent`** — put only if absent; atomic

**Warnings**
- Functions inside `compute`/`merge`/`computeIfAbsent` run while bucket is locked
- Don't do I/O or block
- Don't call other CHM methods on same map (deadlock risk)

**Parallel bulk operations (Java 8+)**
- `forEach(parallelismThreshold, action)` — parallelizes if size exceeds threshold
- `reduce`, `search` also available
- Useful for bulk processing with minimum overhead

**size() approximation**
- CHM's size() returns an approximation
- Maintained as sum of per-bucket counters
- For exact long-valued count: `mappingCount()`

**Collections.synchronizedMap(hashMap)**
- Single-lock wrapper around HashMap
- Every op acquires the one monitor — serialized
- Iteration requires external sync: `synchronized (map) { for (... ) }`
- Compound ops NOT atomic: `if (!m.containsKey(k)) m.put(k, v)` has race
- Slower than CHM under contention
- Only for legacy / low-contention scenarios

**Hashtable — legacy**
- Same semantics as synchronizedMap
- Ancient API
- **Never use in new code**; use CHM

**When to use which**

**Single-threaded**: HashMap

**Multi-threaded**: ConcurrentHashMap (default choice)

**Legacy / simple / low-contention**: Collections.synchronizedMap is fine

**Very specific patterns**: ConcurrentSkipListMap for sorted concurrent, EnumMap synchronized for enum keys

**Migration tip**
- HashMap → CHM: replace null keys/values with sentinels
- Iterate-modify patterns work in CHM without CME
- Compound ops (check-then-put) become atomic via compute/merge

**Recommendation:** Default to **`ConcurrentHashMap`** for any multi-threaded scenario — lock-free reads via volatile, CAS fast path for empty buckets, per-bucket `synchronized` only for collision chains, and a rich set of **atomic compound operations** (`computeIfAbsent`, `compute`, `merge`, `putIfAbsent`). These atomic ops are the main reason to prefer CHM over external synchronization — they're the only way to do thread-safe memoization or counter updates without hand-rolled locks. Remember CHM **forbids null keys and values** — the ambiguity between 'absent' and 'present but null' can't be safely resolved under concurrency; use sentinels when migrating from HashMap. The iterator is **weakly consistent** — no CME, but you may or may not see concurrent changes; for a snapshot, copy the map. Avoid **`Collections.synchronizedMap`** and **`Hashtable`** — both use a single lock that serializes all operations; use them only for legacy code migration. Use **HashMap** only when you know access is single-threaded (e.g., method-local, request-scoped). Don't do I/O or block inside the functions you pass to `compute`/`merge` — the bucket is locked during execution. For parallel bulk operations, use CHM's **`forEach(parallelismThreshold, ...)`** with a sensible threshold; it only parallelizes when worthwhile. The mental model: **HashMap = fast, single-thread; CHM = near-HashMap reads, bucket-scoped writes, safe for anything; synchronizedMap = legacy single-lock fallback**.

groups.heading: HashMap
groups.text: Single-threaded only. No synchronization. Fast. But concurrent writes can corrupt the internal array — causing lost updates, null values, or an infinite resize loop in Java 7 and earlier.

groups.heading: ConcurrentHashMap
groups.text: Thread-safe, designed for concurrency. Uses bucket-level locks in Java 8+ — only the affected segment is locked on write. Reads are lock-free. High throughput under contention.

groups.heading: HashMap
groups.text: Single-threaded code, or when you handle synchronization yourself (local method scope).

groups.heading: ConcurrentHashMap
groups.text: Any shared mutable map. The trap candidates miss: even read-only access to a HashMap being mutated concurrently is unsafe — reads can see a half-resized array.

beats.text: Two threads calling HashMap.put() simultaneously can trigger a resize race. In Java 7, this caused an infinite loop in the linked chain. In Java 8 it's a lost update. ConcurrentHashMap's bucket lock prevents both.

questions.question: Compare Stack vs Queue in Java. Why is the `Stack` class legacy, and what should you use instead?
questions.title: Stack vs Queue in Java — LIFO, FIFO, and Why to Use ArrayDeque Instead
questions.direct_answer: **Stack** is **LIFO (last-in, first-out)** — the most recently pushed item is popped first. **Queue** is **FIFO (first-in, first-out)** — the earliest-added item is removed first. Java has a legacy **`Stack` class** (extends `Vector`, all methods `synchronized`) that **you should NEVER use in new code** — it's slow, has a bloated API (all `Vector` methods are inherited), and violates encapsulation (a stack should not allow random-access indexing, yet you can call `Stack.elementAt(i)`). Java's official recommendation in the `Stack` Javadoc is to use **`Deque` / `ArrayDeque`** instead — it supports `push`, `pop`, `peek` (LIFO) and also `offer`, `poll`, `peek` (FIFO). **For a FIFO queue**: the **`Queue`** interface (implemented by `ArrayDeque`, `LinkedList`, `PriorityQueue`) provides `offer`, `poll`, `peek`. **`ArrayDeque`** is the recommended implementation — **`offerLast`/`pollFirst`** for FIFO, **`offerFirst`/`pollFirst`** for LIFO. All operations are **O(1) amortized**, contiguous memory (cache-friendly), no pointer chasing. **Avoid `LinkedList` as a Queue** — it works but has worse cache locality and memory overhead. **For thread-safe queues**: use `ConcurrentLinkedDeque`, `LinkedBlockingQueue`, `ArrayBlockingQueue`, or `ConcurrentLinkedQueue`. **For priority queues**: `PriorityQueue` (min-heap by default, custom comparator for max-heap). The decision: **LIFO stack** → `Deque<T> stack = new ArrayDeque<>()`, use `push`/`pop`/`peek`. **FIFO queue** → `Queue<T> q = new ArrayDeque<>()`, use `offer`/`poll`/`peek`. **Priority** → `PriorityQueue`. **Concurrent FIFO** → `ConcurrentLinkedQueue` or `LinkedBlockingQueue`. **Concurrent deque** → `ConcurrentLinkedDeque`. **Never** → `Stack`, `Vector`, `Hashtable` (all legacy synchronized). Common operations to know: `push/pop/peek` for stacks; `offer/poll/peek` for queues (`offer`/`poll` return `false`/`null` on full/empty; `add`/`remove` throw exceptions).

sections.title: Stack vs Queue — Core Semantics
sections.content:
| Property | Stack (LIFO) | Queue (FIFO) |
|---|---|---|
| **Acronym** | Last-in, first-out | First-in, first-out |
| **Visual** | Stack of plates — add/remove from top | Line at a checkout — add at back, remove at front |
| **Add operation** | `push(x)` | `offer(x)` / `add(x)` |
| **Remove operation** | `pop()` — returns top | `poll()` / `remove()` — returns head |
| **Peek at next-out** | `peek()` — returns top | `peek()` / `element()` — returns head |
| **Order of removal** | Reverse of insertion | Same as insertion |
| **Use cases** | Undo/redo, function calls, DFS, parenthesis matching, expression eval | Task scheduling, BFS, buffer, producer-consumer |
| **Java legacy class** | `java.util.Stack` — **don't use** | None — `Queue` is an interface |
| **Recommended** | `Deque<T> stack = new ArrayDeque<>()` | `Queue<T> q = new ArrayDeque<>()` |
| **Concurrent** | `ConcurrentLinkedDeque` | `ConcurrentLinkedQueue`, `LinkedBlockingQueue` |

sections.title: Deque as Stack and Queue
Why Java's `Stack` Class Is Legacy
sections.content:
`java.util.Stack` was part of Java 1.0. It has multiple design flaws.

**1. Extends `Vector`** — and `Vector` extends too much API:
```java
Stack<Integer> s = new Stack<>();
s.push(1);
s.push(2);
s.push(3);
int x = s.elementAt(0);   // you can randomly-access index into a 'stack'!
s.set(1, 99);              // you can mutate in the middle!
// All inherited from Vector — breaks stack encapsulation
```
A stack should expose only push/pop/peek. `Stack` exposes the full `Vector` API (100+ methods including `get(int)`, `remove(int)`, `add(int, E)`). Misuse is possible and common.

**2. All methods are `synchronized`**:
- Every `push`, `pop`, `peek` acquires the instance monitor.
- Severe overhead in single-threaded code.
- Doesn't compose: compound operations like 'pop two and compare' need external synchronization anyway.

**3. Slower than `ArrayDeque`**:
- Cache-unfriendly (linked-list-like growth despite being array-backed in old Vector).
- Synchronized overhead on every op.

**4. Official Java recommendation**:
> 'A more complete and consistent set of LIFO stack operations is provided by the `Deque` interface and its implementations, which should be used in preference to this class.'
>
> — `java.util.Stack` Javadoc

**5. Same story for `Vector` and `Hashtable`**:
- `Vector` → use `ArrayList` (or `CopyOnWriteArrayList` / `Collections.synchronizedList` for thread-safety).
- `Hashtable` → use `HashMap` (or `ConcurrentHashMap`).

**Never use in new code**: `Stack`, `Vector`, `Hashtable`, `Dictionary`, `Enumeration`. They're kept for backward compatibility only.

sections.title: ArrayDeque — The Modern Stack and Queue
sections.content:
**`ArrayDeque`** is a resizable-array implementation of `Deque` (double-ended queue). It works as both a stack and a queue.

**As a LIFO stack**:
```java
Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
stack.push(1);    // add to front
stack.push(2);
stack.push(3);
int top = stack.peek();   // 3
int popped = stack.pop(); // 3
// push/pop/peek at the 'top' (front of deque)
```

**As a FIFO queue**:
```java
Queue<Integer> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
queue.offer(1);   // add to back
queue.offer(2);
queue.offer(3);
int head = queue.peek();   // 1
int polled = queue.poll(); // 1
// offer to back, poll from front — FIFO
```

**Full Deque API**:
```java
Deque<Integer> dq = new ArrayDeque<>();
dq.addFirst(1); dq.offerFirst(2);    // add to front (both work; offer returns boolean)
dq.addLast(3);  dq.offerLast(4);     // add to back
dq.removeFirst(); dq.pollFirst();    // remove from front
dq.removeLast();  dq.pollLast();     // remove from back
dq.peekFirst(); dq.peekLast();        // inspect ends
dq.getFirst();  dq.getLast();         // inspect, throw if empty
```

**Performance**:
- All operations: O(1) amortized.
- Array-backed, cache-friendly.
- No pointer chasing (unlike `LinkedList`).
- Circular buffer internally — resize only when full.

**Why not LinkedList?**
- LinkedList implements Deque too but with per-node allocation.
- Poor cache locality (pointer chasing through memory).
- Higher memory overhead per element.
- ArrayDeque is strictly better for stack/queue use unless you need specific list operations.

sections.title: `offer/poll/peek` vs `add/remove/element`
PriorityQueue and Concurrent Alternatives
sections.content:
**`PriorityQueue`** — not FIFO; removes smallest element first (min-heap):
```java
PriorityQueue<Integer> pq = new PriorityQueue<>();
pq.offer(3); pq.offer(1); pq.offer(2);
pq.poll();   // 1 (min)
pq.poll();   // 2
pq.poll();   // 3
```

**Max-heap** — use `Comparator.reverseOrder()`:
```java
PriorityQueue<Integer> maxHeap = new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.reverseOrder());
```

**Custom order**:
```java
PriorityQueue<Task> pq = new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.comparingInt(Task::priority));
```

**Performance**: offer/poll O(log n), peek O(1), **`contains` O(n)**, **`remove(elem)` O(n)**.

**Not thread-safe** — use `PriorityBlockingQueue` for concurrent.

**Concurrent queues**:

**`ConcurrentLinkedQueue`** — unbounded non-blocking FIFO:
- Lock-free (CAS-based).
- Good for high-throughput producer-consumer.

**`ConcurrentLinkedDeque`** — non-blocking deque:
- Same design, both ends accessible.

**`LinkedBlockingQueue`** — optionally bounded blocking FIFO:
- Locks on ends.
- `put`/`take` block if full/empty.
- Classic producer-consumer.

**`ArrayBlockingQueue`** — bounded fixed-size blocking FIFO:
- Array-backed.
- Good for back-pressure-controlled pipelines.

**`SynchronousQueue`** — zero-capacity hand-off:
- Each `put` waits for a matching `take`.
- Used in `Executors.newCachedThreadPool`.

**`LinkedBlockingDeque`**, **`PriorityBlockingQueue`**, **`DelayQueue`**, **`LinkedTransferQueue`** — specialized variants.

**Decision**:
- Simple concurrent FIFO: `ConcurrentLinkedQueue`.
- Bounded / producer-consumer: `LinkedBlockingQueue` / `ArrayBlockingQueue`.
- Priority + concurrent: `PriorityBlockingQueue`.
- Delayed tasks: `DelayQueue`.
- Hand-off zero buffer: `SynchronousQueue`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Stack = LIFO**; **Queue = FIFO**; **Deque** = double-ended (both).
- **Never use `java.util.Stack`**: legacy, synchronized, extends Vector (API bloat).
- **`ArrayDeque`** is the modern replacement for Stack/Queue/Deque.
- **As stack**: `push`/`pop`/`peek` — operate at the head.
- **As queue**: `offer`/`poll`/`peek` — `offer` adds to tail, `poll` removes from head.
- **Two method families**: `offer/poll/peek` (return special value on fail); `add/remove/element` (throw).
- **Prefer `offer/poll/peek`** unless you want exceptions.
- **Don't use `LinkedList`** as Stack/Queue — ArrayDeque has better cache locality.
- **Deque convention**: `push(e)` = `addFirst(e)`, `pop()` = `removeFirst()`, `peek()` = `peekFirst()`.
- **`PriorityQueue`**: min-heap by default; use `Comparator.reverseOrder()` for max.
- **`PriorityQueue.contains` is O(n)**, not O(log n) — common trap.
- **Concurrent queues**: `ConcurrentLinkedQueue` (lock-free), `LinkedBlockingQueue` (blocking, bounded), `ArrayBlockingQueue` (bounded, array-backed), `SynchronousQueue` (hand-off).
- **Don't use**: `Stack`, `Vector`, `Hashtable` — all legacy synchronized.
- **BFS**: Queue. **DFS**: Stack (or recursion).
- **Producer-consumer**: BlockingQueue.
- **Task priority**: PriorityQueue / PriorityBlockingQueue.
- **Undo/redo**: two Stacks (ArrayDeques).

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Stack is LIFO** — last-in, first-out. **Queue is FIFO** — first-in, first-out. **Deque** supports both (double-ended queue).

**Don't use `java.util.Stack`**
- Legacy (Java 1.0)
- All methods synchronized — slow in single-threaded code
- Extends Vector — bloated API including `get(int)`, random-access, `set(int, e)`
- Javadoc itself says 'use Deque instead'
- Same for Vector and Hashtable — never use in new code

**Use ArrayDeque — modern replacement**

**As a stack (LIFO)**
- `push(e)` — add to front
- `pop()` — remove from front
- `peek()` — inspect front
- All O(1) amortized

**As a queue (FIFO)**
- `offer(e)` — add to back
- `poll()` — remove from front
- `peek()` — inspect front
- All O(1) amortized

**Why ArrayDeque over LinkedList**
- Array-backed, cache-friendly
- No pointer-chasing
- Lower memory overhead per element
- Circular buffer internally
- LinkedList works as deque but is strictly worse for stack/queue use

**Two method families — error handling**

**Throwing**
- `add(e)`, `remove()`, `element()`
- Throw IllegalStateException / NoSuchElementException
- Use when empty/full is exceptional

**Special-value**
- `offer(e)`, `poll()`, `peek()`
- Return false / null on failure
- Use for normal flow
- BFS: `while ((Node n = q.poll()) != null) {...}` — loop exits naturally

**Deque convention**
- `push(e)` = `addFirst(e)`
- `pop()` = `removeFirst()`
- `peek()` = `peekFirst()`
- `offer(e)` = `offerLast(e)`
- `poll()` = `pollFirst()`
- So stack ops are at the front; queue offer adds to back, poll removes from front

**Use cases**

**Stack (LIFO)**
- Undo/redo (two stacks)
- Function call evaluation
- DFS (or recursion, which uses call stack)
- Parenthesis matching
- Expression evaluation (postfix, infix)

**Queue (FIFO)**
- Task scheduling
- BFS
- Buffer / pipeline
- Producer-consumer

**PriorityQueue**
- Smallest element first (min-heap)
- `Comparator.reverseOrder()` for max-heap
- offer/poll: O(log n); peek: O(1)
- `contains`: O(n) — common trap
- Not thread-safe — use PriorityBlockingQueue

**Concurrent alternatives**

**ConcurrentLinkedQueue**
- Lock-free, CAS-based
- Unbounded FIFO
- High-throughput

**ConcurrentLinkedDeque**
- Same design, both ends

**LinkedBlockingQueue**
- Optionally bounded
- Blocks on full/empty via put/take
- Classic producer-consumer

**ArrayBlockingQueue**
- Bounded fixed-size
- Array-backed
- Good for back-pressure

**SynchronousQueue**
- Zero-capacity hand-off
- Each put waits for a take
- Used in cached thread pool

**PriorityBlockingQueue**
- Concurrent priority queue

**DelayQueue**
- Elements with delay; poll returns only expired
- For scheduled tasks

**Decision matrix**

- LIFO stack → `Deque<T> stack = new ArrayDeque<>()`, use push/pop/peek
- FIFO queue → `Queue<T> q = new ArrayDeque<>()`, use offer/poll/peek
- Priority smallest first → `PriorityQueue<>` min-heap
- Priority largest first → `PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.reverseOrder())`
- Concurrent FIFO → `ConcurrentLinkedQueue`
- Concurrent deque → `ConcurrentLinkedDeque`
- Bounded producer-consumer → `LinkedBlockingQueue` or `ArrayBlockingQueue`
- Hand-off → `SynchronousQueue`
- Delayed tasks → `DelayQueue`
- Never → `Stack`, `Vector`, `Hashtable`

**Common traps**

**1. Using `Stack` class**
- Legacy, synchronized, API bloat
- Use ArrayDeque

**2. Using LinkedList as stack/queue**
- Works but suboptimal
- ArrayDeque is faster (cache locality)

**3. `PriorityQueue.contains` is O(n)**
- Not O(log n)
- No hash index

**4. Mixing offer/poll with add/remove**
- Different error behavior (return value vs throw)
- Pick one style per context

**5. Not knowing push/pop are at the front in Deque**
- Counterintuitive but standard
- `push` = `addFirst`, not `addLast`

**Recommendation:** For **LIFO stacks**, use **`Deque<T> stack = new ArrayDeque<>()`** with `push`/`pop`/`peek`. For **FIFO queues**, use **`Queue<T> q = new ArrayDeque<>()`** with `offer`/`poll`/`peek`. Never use the legacy **`Stack`** class — it's synchronized, extends `Vector`, and exposes dangerous random-access methods; the Javadoc itself recommends `Deque`. Never use **`LinkedList`** as a stack or queue — **`ArrayDeque`** has far better cache locality (contiguous memory, no pointer chasing) and lower memory overhead. Prefer **`offer`/`poll`/`peek`** (return special value on fail) over `add`/`remove`/`element` (throw) for normal flow; the special-value variants compose better with loops. For **priority** (smallest-first or custom order), use **`PriorityQueue`** — but remember **`contains` is O(n)**, not O(log n). For **concurrent** scenarios: **`ConcurrentLinkedQueue`** for lock-free FIFO, **`LinkedBlockingQueue`** for bounded producer-consumer, **`ConcurrentLinkedDeque`** for bi-directional lock-free, **`SynchronousQueue`** for direct hand-off. Know the **Deque convention**: `push(e)` = `addFirst(e)`, `pop()` = `removeFirst()` — stack ops operate at the front. Use **BFS with Queue** and **DFS with Stack (or recursion)** — the standard algorithmic pairings. The mental model: **Deque is the universal tool** — it's both a stack and a queue; `ArrayDeque` is the fast default; specialized implementations only when concurrency, priority, blocking, or delay semantics are needed.
